prompt: You just turned on VoiceOver or NVDA and tabbed to the checkbox from the lesson (a <label> correctly associated via for/id, with aria-hidden="true" applied to it). What did you actually hear announced?

options.text: The checkbox and its label are both announced correctly
Only the checkbox state ('not checked') is announced — no label at all
The label is announced quietly, then the checkbox state
The screen reader skips the control entirely

hints: aria-hidden hides an element and all its descendants from assistive tech — including a label element it's applied to directly.
Programmatic association (for/id) links the label in the DOM, but doesn't make it exempt from aria-hidden.
explanation: aria-hidden="true" on a <label> removes it from the accessibility tree entirely. Even though the label is correctly associated with the input via for/id, a screen reader will only announce the input's role and state ('checkbox, not checked') — the label text is never read, so the user has no way to know what they're checking.

prompt: You just put your mouse aside and tabbed through the lesson's page — a <nav> written after <main> in the HTML, but placed visually above it via flex-direction: column-reverse. Where did your keyboard focus actually go right after the logo?

options.text: Tab order matches the visual order — nav is reached first
Tab order follows the DOM — main is reached before nav, regardless of visual position
The browser automatically reorders tab sequence to match CSS
Focus becomes trapped inside main and never reaches nav

hints: CSS properties like flex-direction change what's rendered where on screen — they don't touch the underlying DOM.
Keyboard tab order is determined by DOM position, not by pixels on the page.
explanation: Tab order always follows DOM order, never visual/rendered order. CSS reordering (flex-direction, absolute positioning, grid order, etc.) can make a page look correct to a sighted mouse user while keyboard users experience a completely different, illogical sequence — main content before navigation, in this case. This is why keyboard testing has to be done by physically tabbing through a page, not just by looking at it.

prompt: What happens to the accessibility tree when aria-hidden="true" is applied directly to a <label> element associated with an input?

options.text: The label and its input become permanently detached; no association survives regardless of for/id or nesting
The label is removed from the accessibility tree entirely — it contributes nothing to the input's accessible name, regardless of for/id association
aria-hidden on a label has no effect because labels are inherently non-decorative
The label remains in the accessibility tree but becomes non-narrated

explanation: Applying aria-hidden="true" to a <label> removes it from the accessibility tree. Even though the for/id association is structurally intact in the DOM, the label contributes no accessible name — a screen reader lands on the input and announces only its role and state (e.g. 'checkbox, not checked'), with no label text at all.

prompt: A web page uses CSS flexbox with 'order: 3' on the first button, 'order: 1' on the second, and 'order: 2' on the third. In what tab order will these buttons receive focus?

options.text: Only the element with 'order: 1' is focusable; others are skipped
First, second, third (DOM source order)
Third, then first, then second (as rendered visually)
Second, then third, then first (CSS visual order)

explanation: Tab order always follows DOM source order unless tabindex is explicitly used to override it. CSS flexbox 'order' affects visual layout but not sequential focus navigation.

prompt: When testing keyboard navigation without a mouse, which behavior confirms correct focus management on a custom dropdown widget?

options.text: Once opened, the dropdown options receive focus only when using Arrow keys; pressing Esc closes the menu and returns focus to the trigger button
Focus moves into the dropdown options on Enter, but pressing Escape does not close it or restore focus
The dropdown options are skipped entirely until Tab is pressed repeatedly many times
Pressing Tab moves focus past the trigger button, and pressing Shift+Tab does not return to it

explanation: Proper keyboard handling requires focus to be programmatically moved *within* the widget using arrow keys while Escape returns control and focus to the trigger element — a testable behavior only by manual keyboard navigation.

prompt: A developer added aria-hidden="true" to the entire <header> section. What effect does this have on screen readers?

options.text: The header's contents are still accessible via landmark navigation (e.g., JAWS + H)
The entire header subtree is excluded from the accessibility tree and not announced
All content in the header becomes narrated with a prefix 'hidden'
Only visible elements inside are hidden; focusable links remain navigable

explanation: aria-hidden="true" on a container removes all descendants from the accessibility tree, regardless of visibility or interactivity. Screen readers will not announce them.

prompt: Which statement about label-input association is *technically* true when testing manually with a screen reader?

options.text: If only the 'for' attribute is present and the 'id' doesn’t match, the input is still labeled by whatever text immediately precedes it visually
A <label> with matching for/id or proper nesting must exist in the accessibility tree to be announced; aria-hidden on it prevents labeling
Screen readers use visual proximity alone to infer labels, so no programmatic association is required
A <label> nested inside the <input>'s parent <div> but not explicitly associated via for/id will still be announced as the input's label

explanation: Labels require either HTML association (for/id or nesting) *and* must remain in the accessibility tree; aria-hidden on a label removes that labeling function.

prompt: A modal dialog's close button receives focus via JavaScript when the dialog opens, and subsequent Tab presses move to interactive elements *inside* the dialog. What must also be true for proper keyboard accessibility?

options.text: Pressing Shift+Tab from the first focusable element should move focus into browser UI or past top of page
Only the close button is focus-trapped; other interactive elements use normal flow

Wrapping only needs to work in the forward Tab direction — it's acceptable for Shift+Tab from the first element to leave the dialog and reach the page behind it

explanation: Focus trapping ensures keyboard users cannot tab to background content while a modal is active, which must be verified by manual keyboard-only navigation testing.

prompt: If an input element has tabindex="0" and a sibling <span> also has tabindex="0", how does focus navigate between them?

options.text: Elements with tabindex="0" are skipped unless explicitly navigated via Tab navigation only once
Focus follows DOM order: whichever appears earlier in the source order gets focus first
Tab order is determined by their visual rendering (e.g., absolute positioning)
Both receive focus simultaneously when clicked, but tab key skips both until next element

explanation: Elements with tabindex="0" are included in sequential focus navigation in DOM order — not visual or rendering order.

prompt: What is the consequence of using aria-hidden on a button that has visible text content?

options.text: The button remains focusable and announced, but only with screen readers that support ARIA
Its parent containers inherit aria-hidden and also become hidden
The button becomes clickable but is not announced to screen reader users
It becomes unfocusable and removed from the tab order entirely

explanation: aria-hidden removes an element from the accessibility tree, so screen readers do not announce it — but the button remains focusable if keyboard-accessible via tabindex or natural placement.

prompt: In a complex page where elements are visually stacked using position: absolute, what determines their tab order?

options.text: The z-index stacking context: lower z-index gets focus first
DOM source order only, regardless of position or visibility settings
The visual layering as seen in browser developer tools (right to left)
Only elements in the topmost z-index layer are focusable; others require mouse click

explanation: Focus order is unaffected by CSS positioning like absolute/flex/grid — it strictly follows DOM source unless tabindex overrides are applied.

prompt: A developer uses aria-label="Close" on a close button, but omits visible text. What is the likely impact for screen reader users?

options.text: aria-label is ignored on buttons; screen readers fall back to inner text or DOM siblings
Visual users see no label, so screen readers should also skip announcing anything
Screen readers will announce 'close, button' only if the button has focusable semantics
The aria-label will be used as the accessible name, but only if the element supports it (e.g., button, link)

explanation: aria-label provides an accessible name if the element supports it (like button), but its absence of visible text may still cause discoverability issues for sighted keyboard users.

prompt: Which test confirms that a carousel's previous/next controls are correctly labeled for screen readers?

options.text: They are skipped during navigation but visible in developer tool inspection
Using screen reader's navigation shortcut (e.g., rotor), the controls appear as 'button' type with descriptive names
Pressing Enter once opens them into a new context before moving again
Pressing Tab reveals them as focusable, and pressing Space triggers movement — but no name is announced

prompt: A checkbox has both a <label> and aria-describedby pointing to additional instructions. How do screen readers typically announce this?

options.text: The full text is concatenated without pause: 'Enable notifications to receive updates about your order'
The screen reader speaks only aria-describedby if present, overriding the label
Label + role + state first, then additional description upon navigation or context change
Only the label text is announced; aria-describedby is ignored unless explicitly navigated

explanation: Screen readers announce the accessible name (label) first, then the description only when explicitly accessed or upon focus entry — not always in a single line.

prompt: If an element's CSS includes pointer-events: none, how does it affect keyboard navigation?

options.text: It remains focusable only if it is a form control like <input> or <button>
It can still receive focus via script or sequential navigation but does not respond to clicks
It becomes non-focusable and is skipped in tab order
The element disappears from the DOM entirely for assistive tech

explanation: pointer-events: none disables mouse interaction but does not affect tab navigation — elements can still be focused via keyboard, requiring programmatic focus handling.

prompt: When an <input> lacks a visible label but has aria-label, what does screen reader testing typically reveal?

options.text: Screen readers announce both inner text and aria-label concatenated
It's not labeled at all unless nested inside <label>
The aria-label serves as the accessible name and is announced on focus or context
The input is announced only with role (e.g., 'edit'), and the aria-label is ignored

prompt: A page uses JavaScript to dynamically insert a new <button> into the DOM after initial load. When does it become part of the tab order?

After a setTimeout of 500ms or longer to ensure accessibility tree sync

explanation: Dynamically inserted elements with native interactivity (e.g., button) become focusable immediately upon insertion — verified by tabbing after DOM mutation.

prompt: A table uses <th> headers but they have aria-hidden="true". What happens when navigating cells with a screen reader?

options.text: Headers are announced after cell data using reverse reference logic

prompt: Which manual test confirms correct focus order when using CSS to visually reorder elements via 'flex-direction: row-reverse'?

Tabbing through items follows visual screen order (right-to-left)

prompt: An <a> element has href="#" and aria-hidden="false". What does that do?

The link becomes focusable only via screen reader virtual cursor, not keyboard Tab
It forces screen readers to announce the link even if it’s empty
It enables assistive tech to navigate only the link, skipping surrounding content

explanation: aria-hidden="false" has no effect unless applied to a child of an ancestor with aria-hidden="true" — it doesn’t re-expose hidden content or alter default behavior.

prompt: When testing a progress indicator with role="progressbar", what must be present for accurate screen reader announcement?

innerText with numeric value in % is sufficient alone
aria-label or accessible name via-labelledby, plus aria-valuenow and either aria-valuemax or aria-valuetext
Only aria-valuenow and aria-valuemin are required; aria-valuemax is optional

prompt: Which behavior demonstrates that focus is correctly managed when closing an open modal dialog?

Focus remains in the modal’s last active element until another tab or click occurs
The entire page receives focus again as a single unit

explanation: Returning focus to the control that opened the dialog is essential for contextual continuity — confirmed only by manually testing keyboard-only navigation.

prompt:
A signup form has two checkboxes, written by two different developers: ```html
``` Only ONE of these two checkboxes will announce a label when a screen reader user tabs to it. Which one is broken, exactly why, and what would VoiceOver or NVDA actually announce landing on it? Then fix the broken markup.
hints: Compare the for attribute on each label against the id on its matching input, character by character — don't assume they match just because they look similar.
Programmatic association via for/id requires an exact string match; even one missing character breaks it completely.
For the broken one, predict exactly what gets announced — compare it to what the lesson's aria-hidden example announced.
explanation: The first checkbox (marketing-opt-in) works fine — for="marketing-opt-in" matches id="marketing-opt-in" exactly. The second is broken: the label says for="sms-opt-in" but the input's id is "sms-optin" (missing the hyphen), so there is no programmatic association at all, despite looking correct at a glance. A screen reader landing on that input announces only "checkbox, not checked" — the exact same silent failure the lesson demonstrated with aria-hidden on a label, just caused by a typo in the id instead. The fix is a one-character change: `<input type="checkbox" id="sms-opt-in">` so the id matches the label's for attribute exactly.

prompt:
Two more checkbox implementations from the same codebase: ```html
``` Which version will screen reader users hear a label for, and which won't? Explain the mechanism for each — don't just say "aria-hidden hides it," explain precisely what happens to the accessibility tree in Version B.
hints: aria-hidden removes the element it's applied to AND every descendant from the accessibility tree — check what's actually a descendant of the aria-hidden element in Version B.
Version A uses a different, also-valid way of associating a label with its input — does the lesson call this technique out by name?
For each version, predict exactly what VoiceOver/NVDA would announce landing on the checkbox.
explanation:
Version A works: wrapping the input inside the <label> element (rather than using for/id) is the third valid association technique the lesson names alongside for/id and aria-labelledby — the label text "I agree to the Terms of Service" is correctly in the accessibility tree and gets announced with the checkbox's role and state.

Version B is broken, and for a subtler reason than the lesson's original example: aria-hidden="true" isn't on the <label> itself here — it's on the <div> that wraps the label. But aria-hidden removes its target AND every descendant from the accessibility tree, and the label is a descendant of that div. So the label is just as invisible to assistive tech as if aria-hidden had been placed directly on it — the checkbox announces only "checkbox, not checked," with zero label, exactly like the lesson's original broken example.

prompt: Two custom checkbox widgets, each pairing a decorative icon with label text: ```html ``` Both widgets use aria-hidden somewhere. One is genuinely accessible; one is broken. Identify which is which, explain precisely what a screen reader announces for each, and state the general rule for when aria-hidden on part of a label is fine versus when it breaks the control entirely.
hints: aria-hidden hides exactly the element it's applied to, plus everything inside it — figure out precisely which element each snippet applies it to.
One developer correctly hid only a decorative icon; the other hid the icon's entire container, including the real label text along with it.
For each widget, ask: after stripping out everything aria-hidden removes, what accessible name is left for the input?
explanation:
Widget 1 is correct. aria-hidden="true" is on the <span> icon only — a legitimate, recommended pattern for suppressing purely decorative content from being announced (without it, a screen reader might read "crescent moon emoji, Enable dark mode, checkbox, not checked" — noisy and confusing). The surrounding label text "Enable dark mode" is not a descendant of the aria-hidden span, so it stays in the accessibility tree, and the label is still properly associated via for/id. VoiceOver announces: "Enable dark mode, checkbox, not checked."

Widget 2 is broken. aria-hidden="true" is on the <label> element itself — the ancestor of both the icon span and the text "Enable compact layout." Because aria-hidden removes its target and every descendant, the entire label subtree — icon and text alike — is pulled from the accessibility tree. The checkbox announces only "checkbox, not checked," with no label at all. The developer likely intended to hide just the icon, like Widget 1, but put aria-hidden on the wrong element.

General rule: aria-hidden on decorative content nested *inside* an accessible label is a good pattern. aria-hidden on the label itself — or on any ancestor that also contains the real accessible text — takes the text down with it and breaks the control.

prompt:
A checkout page uses this HTML and CSS: ```html
``` ```css .button-row { display: flex; flex-direction: row-reverse; /* visually: Continue renders on the left, Back on the right */ } ``` You put your mouse aside and tab through the page. Which button receives focus first — Back or Continue? Is this a bug? If so, fix it, and explain why fixing it with more CSS wouldn't be the right approach.
hints: Tab order is determined by source order in the HTML — never by CSS flex-direction.
Ask: if I only had a keyboard and never looked at the screen, which button would I land on first?
The fix has to happen in the HTML file, not the CSS file — think about why.
explanation:
"Back" receives focus first, because it's written first in the HTML — tab order follows DOM order regardless of flex-direction, exactly as the lesson's nav/main example demonstrated. This is a real bug: a sighted keyboard user sees "Continue" on the left and "Back" on the right (because of row-reverse), so they'd expect Tab to reach Continue first if anything — instead they land on Back first, out of step with the visual order they're looking at. It's invisible to a mouse-only QA pass because the page looks completely correct.

Fix: reorder the actual markup — swap the two <button> elements so <button class="btn-continue"> comes before <button class="btn-back"> in the HTML — so DOM order matches the intended visual/tab order. Patching this further in CSS can never work: flex-direction only ever changes rendering, never the underlying DOM order that Tab actually follows.

prompt:
A footer, with its HTML in this order: ```html
Privacy Terms
Twitter Instagram
``` ```css footer { display: grid; grid-template-areas: "social newsletter legal"; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; } .social-links { grid-area: social; } .newsletter-signup { grid-area: newsletter; } nav { grid-area: legal; } ``` Visually this shows social links on the left, newsletter form in the middle, legal nav on the right. A teammate says: "It's fine — I put aria-label='Legal' on the nav so screen reader users can jump straight to it with landmark navigation, so tab order doesn't matter here." Is the teammate right? Trace the actual tab order a keyboard user experiences, and explain specifically what the aria-label does and doesn't solve.
hints: Landmark navigation (jumping directly to a labeled region) and sequential Tab navigation are two different ways users move through a page — fixing one doesn't fix the other.
grid-template-areas works exactly like flex-direction and the CSS order property: it changes rendering only, never DOM/tab order.
Trace the actual HTML source order first, ignoring the CSS entirely, to find the real tab sequence.
explanation:
The teammate is only half right. aria-label="Legal" does make the <nav> landmark identifiable and independently reachable for screen reader users who jump directly between landmarks — that part is genuinely useful. But it does nothing for a keyboard-only user tabbing sequentially through the page, and it does nothing to fix the actual tab order.

grid-template-areas, like flex-direction and the CSS order property covered in the lesson, only changes visual placement — DOM/tab order still follows source order in the HTML, which here is: nav (legal links) first, then the newsletter form, then social links. A sighted keyboard user reading left to right expects social → newsletter → legal, but Tab actually delivers legal → newsletter → social — reversed from what they see. The aria-label solves a different problem (targeted landmark jumping) than the one that actually exists (sequential tab order mismatching visual order).

Fix: reorder the markup itself so the DOM sequence is social-links, then newsletter-signup, then nav — matching the visual left-to-right order. The grid-template-areas CSS can stay exactly as-is for layout; it should never be relied on to fix focus order.

prompt:
You're reviewing a pull request that redesigns a pricing table. The diff only touches CSS — it adds `order: -1` to the "Recommended" plan's card so it visually renders first among three pricing cards, without touching the HTML at all. The PR description says: "Moved Recommended plan to the front visually, LGTM to merge."

Write the code review comment you would leave. It must: (1) state precisely what will break for keyboard users and why, (2) say what you'd personally verify by hand before approving — not just what an automated scanner would report, and (3) give the specific fix, including what should change and what should NOT need to change.
hints: Think about what an automated accessibility scanner would and wouldn't catch here — that's exactly why manual testing matters for this class of bug.
CSS order and DOM/tab order are two completely separate systems — changing one never changes the other.
A strong review comment names the specific user-facing symptom (what a keyboard user experiences), not just "this violates a rule."
explanation:
A strong review comment covers:

1. **What breaks**: `order: -1` is a purely visual CSS property — it changes rendering position but never DOM/tab order, which always follows HTML source order. If the Recommended card is still third in the markup, a keyboard user tabbing through the page reaches the other two plans before reaching Recommended, even though it now visually renders first — completely out of sync with what they're looking at. This passes an automated scanner with zero errors, since there's no ARIA or semantic violation here — the only way to catch it is to physically tab through the rendered page (mouse aside) and confirm the sequence you land on matches the sequence you see.

2. **What I'd verify by hand**: I'd tab through the live preview myself and note exactly which card receives focus first, second, third — not trust that `order: -1` did what its name implies for keyboard users.

3. **The fix**: move the Recommended card's markup to be first in the HTML source, matching its new visual position. Once DOM order matches visual order, the `order: -1` can be removed entirely — don't stack another CSS property on top to patch a problem that only exists because the source order itself is wrong.

hints: Trace both directions separately — Tab forward from the last element, and Shift+Tab backward from the first element — don't assume the code handles them symmetrically.
Look at exactly what the keydown handler checks: does it ever read e.shiftKey anywhere?
A real trap has to intercept the boundary case in both directions, not just one.
Split the lifecycle into two separate moments and check each independently: what happens the instant the modal opens, and what happens the instant it closes.
Is anything in openModal() actually moving focus into the dialog, or does it just make the dialog visible?
document.body isn't focusable by default — think about what calling focus() on it actually accomplishes.
Don't just re-check the Tab-wrap logic — it's already correct here. Look at every interactive-looking element and ask: can I actually reach it and activate it using only a keyboard?
The 'focusable' NodeList only queries for 'button' elements — check whether every clickable-looking element in the markup is actually a <button>.
Check every place closeModal() is wired up — is there a keydown listener for Escape anywhere, or only onclick attributes?
explanation:
Two real problems remain, even though the trap logic and focus restoration are both solid:

1. **The close "×" is unreachable by keyboard.** It's a `<div class="close-x" onclick="closeModal()">`, not a <button> or <a href>. Divs aren't natively focusable or keyboard-operable — no default tabindex, no keydown-triggered click. Worse, `focusable` is built with `querySelectorAll('#delete-modal button')`, which only matches real <button> elements — the close div isn't in that NodeList at all, so it's silently excluded from the tab cycle entirely. A mouse user sees and can click the × fine; a keyboard user can never reach it and has no way to know it exists, because Tab just cycles between Delete and Cancel.

2. **There's no Escape key handling anywhere.** closeModal() is only ever wired to onclick attributes. A correctly-implemented dialog should close on Escape and return focus to the trigger — here, Escape does nothing at all, even though clicking Cancel and the trap wrapping both work.

Fix priority: the unreachable close button first — it's a complete "this functionality doesn't exist for keyboard users" gap (either give the div `tabindex="0"` plus a keydown handler, or, better, make it a real <button> and include it in the `focusable` NodeList so the trap wraps around it too). Escape-to-close is the close second priority — genuinely expected behavior that's simply missing, but Cancel and Delete remain independently reachable via Tab, so it's a smaller gap than a control that's completely unreachable.

prompt:
An audit of a checkout flow produces these two findings:

**A.** The company logo in the header has `alt="logo"` rather than the company name.

**B.** When card validation fails, the field gets a red border and the text *Invalid* appears next to it, inserted into the DOM with no live region and no focus move.

Both are real. Which one belongs at the top of the report, and on what basis?

options.text: A — it fails 1.1.1 Non-text Content, a Level A criterion, and A comes before AA
B — a screen reader user gets no indication the payment failed, so the task stops
A — alt text is the most common accessibility complaint, so it affects more people
Neither — they are both Level A, so they carry the same severity by definition

hints: Ask what each one costs the person: what can they no longer do?
Conformance level describes which criterion was broken. It says nothing about what the break costs.
explanation:
B stops the task. A screen reader user submits the form, hears nothing change, and has no way to know the payment was rejected or why — the flow simply appears not to respond. A is a genuine 1.1.1 failure and worth fixing, but a user who hears "logo" instead of the company name loses a little context and finishes checkout anyway.

The distractor worth naming is the third one: alt text being the most *reported* issue reflects what automated scanners can detect, not what harms users most. Frequency in scan reports is a property of the tools, not of the barrier.

prompt:
Here is a finding as it was actually written in a real audit:

> **Issue 23 (AA):** 2.4.7 Focus Visible — focus indicator missing on some elements. Fix the CSS.

A developer picks this up two weeks later, with no access to you. Rewrite it so they can act on it without asking a single follow-up question. Then say, in one sentence, what a product manager reading only your first line would learn.
hints: Which elements, on which page, in which state? "Some" is the word doing all the damage here.
What can a keyboard user no longer do as a result? That sentence is what the product manager reads.
A reproduction path is: where to start, what to press, what you see, what you expected.
explanation:
A usable rewrite names the task impact first, then the specifics: something like — *A keyboard user cannot tell where they are in the checkout form. On /checkout, tabbing from the email field onward, no visible focus indicator appears on the four input fields or the Pay button (Chrome 122 / Firefox 124, macOS and Windows). The site's reset stylesheet sets `outline: none` on `input, button` at line 41 of base.css with no replacement style. Expected: a visible indicator meeting 1.4.11 contrast against the field background. WCAG 2.4.7 (AA).*

The first sentence is the one a product manager reads, and it has to be about a person and a task, not about a criterion number. "Fails 2.4.7" tells them nothing they can prioritise with. "A keyboard user cannot tell where they are while paying you" does.

prompt: Sort each of these findings into the cheapest method that would reliably catch it. "Reliably" is doing work here — a scanner occasionally stumbling onto something doesn't count.

items.text: An in the product grid has no alt attribute
Body text renders at 3.1:1 against its background
A form field's <label> points at an id that doesn't exist
Every product image has alt="product image"
Tab order jumps from the header to the footer and back to the sidebar
A modal announces correctly but focus is never moved into it
The word "submit" is used for a button that saves a draft, confusing everyone who tries it
Experienced screen reader users abandon the flow because the heading structure gives no sense of where they are

hints: A scanner can compare two colour values and check whether an attribute exists. It cannot judge whether a word is the right word.
If answering the question requires knowing what the content means, it isn't automatable.
If answering it requires knowing what a real person did next, it isn't a manual audit either.
explanation:
The line between the first two columns is **meaning**. A scanner can tell you `alt` is missing; it cannot tell you `alt="product image"` is useless, because checking that requires knowing what the image shows. Same with labels: present-and-associated is machine-checkable, *accurate* is not.

The line between the second two is **behaviour**. A skilled manual reviewer can tell you the heading structure is flat and that this will make orientation hard. Only watching real users tells you they give up at step three because of it, and that is the finding that changes a roadmap.

prompt: A client says: "We run axe on every build and it's been clean for six months, so we're accessible." True or false — and justify your answer in a way the client could act on.

config.statement: A consistently clean automated scan means a product is accessible.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and gives a reason a client could act on — not just which way the answer falls.

hints: What proportion of barriers is the tool even attempting to detect?
What would a clean scan on a page that is entirely unusable by keyboard look like?
The client needs a next step, not just a correction.
explanation:
False — and the useful reply is not "scanners only catch 30%", it's a demonstration. A page can pass every automated check while being completely unusable: semantic HTML throughout, perfect contrast, every image labelled, and a checkout flow where focus is never moved into the payment dialog, so a screen reader user never learns it opened.

A clean scan is genuinely worth having. It means the mechanically-detectable class of defects is under control, which is real and not nothing. It says close to nothing about whether the tasks on the site can be completed. The actionable next step is a keyboard-only pass on the three highest-value journeys — a few hours, no tooling budget, and it will produce findings.

prompt: A reviewer who has used NVDA daily for six years and a reviewer who learned it last month audit the same product page. Both are competent and thorough. Which difference in their findings is most likely, and why?

options.text: The experienced reviewer finds more missing-label defects, because they know the criteria better
The experienced reviewer flags things that technically announce correctly but are unusable at real navigation speed
The new reviewer finds more, because they notice things an experienced user has learned to work around
There is no reliable difference — both are following the same checklist

hints: Which of these differences is about the standard, and which is about how people actually move through a page?
Two of these options describe real effects. Only one is the *most likely* difference.
explanation:
The second option. Missing labels are found equally by anyone who checks; that's checklist work. The difference fluency makes is in the middle ground — a heading structure that is technically valid and useless for orientation, a live region that announces but interrupts, a control whose accessible name is correct and unpronounceable. Those are only visible to someone who navigates by headings and landmarks at speed rather than tabbing through linearly.

The third option is not wrong as a phenomenon — experienced users genuinely do normalise barriers they've worked around for years, and that is a real failure mode worth guarding against. But it makes an experienced reviewer *miss* things, not find more, so it doesn't answer the question asked.

The fourth is the assumption this lesson exists to argue against. If findings were checklist output, fluency would be irrelevant and an automated scan would be sufficient.

prompt: Match each reader of your audit to the thing they most need from it. Each reader needs everything eventually — match them to what they need *first*, in the first thirty seconds.

pairs.right: Reproduction steps, environment, and the specific element
The pattern that caused it, not the instance
Which user journey is blocked, and for whom
Conformance level, criterion cited, and the current exposure
Whether the accessibility statement matches reality

hints: Ask what decision each person is about to make. The thing they need first is whatever that decision turns on.
The designer is not going to fix one button — they own the component every button comes from.
explanation:
One audit, five readers, five different first questions. This is why the standard report structure exists: an executive summary that answers the product owner and legal, findings that answer the developer, and a grouping by root cause that answers the designer.

The procurement case is the one people forget, and it's increasingly where accessibility decisions actually get made — before a product is bought, by someone comparing an accessibility statement against an audit. If your report is the evidence in that comparison, its honesty about scope matters more than its length.

prompt:
You have committed to auditing five user journeys in two weeks. On day three you have a crash and lose four working days. You now have four days for work you scoped at nine.

Write the message you send the client. Then say which parts of the audit you would cut and why — being specific about what the cut costs them.
hints: What does the client need to be able to decide? Give them that, not an apology.
Cutting journeys and cutting depth are different trade-offs with different consequences. Which one preserves the audit's honesty?
There is a version of this message that offers a choice rather than announcing one.
explanation:
The strong version does three things: states the new reality in one line without a medical account, offers a specific choice, and names the cost of each option.

Something like: *"I've lost four working days and have four remaining against nine days of scoped work. Two options. (a) I audit three of the five journeys at full depth — you get findings you can act on immediately, and two journeys stay unexamined, which I'd state plainly in the scope section. (b) I cover all five at reduced depth — automated plus keyboard only, no screen reader pass — which will surface fewer and shallower findings across more surface. I recommend (a): a shallow pass across everything tends to produce a report that reads as reassuring, and this product's risk is concentrated in checkout. Happy to go with (b) if breadth matters more for your deadline."*

The reasoning behind that recommendation is the part worth internalising. Reduced-depth-everywhere is the more dangerous deliverable: it produces a document that *looks* like full coverage and quietly certifies journeys nobody properly examined. Fewer journeys, honestly scoped, is the option that keeps the audit true.

What doesn't belong: an explanation of your health, an apology longer than a sentence, or a silent delivery of reduced work at the original scope wording.

prompt: A page's only navigation is a set of `<div>` elements with click handlers, styled as links. Which of these is the *task-level* statement of the barrier?

options.text: The navigation fails 2.1.1 Keyboard and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
A keyboard or screen reader user cannot move between sections of the site at all
The divs should be anchor elements

hints: One of these is a citation, one is a fix, one is a consequence.
explanation: The second. The first is the citation and the third is the recommended fix — both belong in the finding, underneath a first line that says what a person can no longer do.

prompt: True or false: a Level A failure is always more severe than a Level AA failure.

config.statement: Level A failures are always more severe than Level AA failures.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and gives a reason a client could act on — not just which way the answer falls.

hints: Conformance level describes how fundamental a criterion is considered, across all content.
Think of a Level A failure on a decorative element versus an AA failure in a checkout.
explanation: False. Conformance level is a property of the criterion, not of the instance. A missing `alt` on a decorative image is a Level A failure that blocks nobody; insufficient contrast on the only error message in a payment form is Level AA and can stop a transaction. Severity comes from impact, frequency and whether a workaround exists — level is an input to that judgement, not a substitute for it.

prompt: Sort each observation by whether it is a *conformance failure*, a *barrier with no clean criterion*, or *both*.

items.text: A decorative divider image has alt="divider" instead of an empty alt
The form clears all entered data after a 15-minute timeout, with no warning
The only way to dismiss a promotional overlay is a 12x12px close button with no accessible name
Eligibility questions are written at a reading level most applicants can't parse under stress
A required field's asterisk is conveyed by red colour alone

hints: Ask two separate questions of each: does a criterion clearly cover it, and does it stop the task?
explanation: The middle column is the one this module exists for. Timeouts that destroy work and content nobody can parse under stress are among the most common reasons real people abandon government and healthcare services, and neither has a criterion you can point at without an argument. They still go in the report.

prompt: Which of these findings could a well-configured automated scanner detect reliably?

options.text: A `<label>` whose `for` attribute references an id that does not exist on the page
A `<label>` correctly associated with an input, whose text describes the wrong field
A form where focus is never moved to the first error after failed validation
A heading structure that is valid but conveys nothing about the page

hints: Which of these can be decided by looking at the markup, without knowing what anything means?
explanation: Only the first. A broken `for`/`id` reference is a pure markup property. The other three need, respectively: understanding what the field is for, observing runtime behaviour, and judging whether text is meaningful. None of those is available to static analysis.

prompt: Put the five steps of turning an observation into a finding into order.

items: Name the task the user was trying to complete
Name the access method affected, and the environment it was observed in
State exactly where the task stops
State what the user is left with — is there another path?
Cite the success criterion, if one applies

hints: The citation is not the first step, and the reason it isn't is the point of the whole procedure.
explanation: Running this backwards — starting from a criterion and hunting for instances — is what produces audits that are technically complete and practically useless. Task first, citation last.

prompt: Match each audit reader to the section of the report they will read first.

pairs.right: The individual finding with reproduction steps
The scope statement and its exclusions

hints: Each of these people is about to make a different decision.
explanation: The procurement reviewer is the one most often designed for last and most often the one whose decision carries the most money. They are reading to find out whether an accessibility claim is backed by anything.

prompt:
A client asks: "Our developers already run an accessibility linter in their editor and we have axe in CI. What would a manual audit add that we're not already getting?"

Answer in under 120 words, without being condescending and without dismissing what they've built.
hints: They have genuinely done something valuable. Say so first, and mean it.
One concrete example of a barrier their setup cannot see will do more than any statistic.
explanation:
A strong answer credits the existing work, then makes the boundary concrete rather than statistical: their tooling covers the class of defects decidable from markup, and covers it continuously, which is better than most organisations manage. What it cannot see is anything requiring meaning, layout or runtime behaviour — so a checkout where focus is never moved into the payment dialog will pass every check they run and be unusable with a screen reader. Then offer the cheap next step: a keyboard-only pass on the top journeys, a few hours, no new tooling.

What weakens an answer: leading with a percentage, or implying their CI setup is theatre. It isn't.

prompt: True or false: because you use a screen reader daily, you are qualified to judge whether an interface's cognitive load is acceptable.

config.statement: Daily screen reader use qualifies a reviewer to judge cognitive accessibility.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and gives a reason a client could act on — not just which way the answer falls.

hints: These are different access needs with different evidence behind them.
The answer should be specific about what you *are* qualified to say.
explanation: False, and the useful version of the answer says what you *can* claim. Screen reader fluency gives you real authority on navigation, announcement quality, structure and operability — write those with confidence. Cognitive load is a different access need; you can review it against known guidance and flag concerns, but "is this comprehensible under stress" is settled by testing with the people it's for. Saying so in the scope section is a mark of a serious reviewer, not a limitation to hide.
